title: Rohatsu
hookLine: the week of sitting before December 8

lines: WHAT SHOWS UP IN A LONG SIT?
cards: What shows up when you sit still for a long time? Not two minutes. Days.

In Japanese Zen, the week that ends on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening is called Rohatsu: a week of sitting, from before dawn into the night. Last year you met its end, the last night and the morning star.
This year, stay in the middle, the long hours when the mind brings out everything it has. An old poem has a name for all of it.

teach.b: The poem is the Padhana Sutta, the discourse on striving, in the Sutta Nipata. The young seeker is by a river, worn thin from effort, and Mara comes to him. Not with weapons.
Kindly. You're thin, he says. You're close to death.
Live, and do good deeds. Why wear yourself out? It's a reasonable voice.
The seeker answers by naming Mara's army, one troop at a time. Desires. Discontent.
Hunger and thirst. Craving. Sloth and drowsiness.
Gain, fame and honor, and praising yourself while looking down on others. There isn't a monster in that list.

teach.h: IT'S THE INSIDE OF A LONG SIT.
teach.b: It's the inside of a long sit: aching legs, and the voice that says this is pointless. Hunger an hour before lunch. Sleep pulling at the eyelids after midday.
Doubt asking who you think you are. A little pride, too, about how well you're sitting. The poem's weapon isn't force.

teach.h: SEE IT, NAME IT, DON'T GET UP.
teach.b: The seeker will break this army with wisdom, the way a stone breaks an unbaked clay pot: see each troop clearly, name it, and not get up. In the poem's own picture, he would rather fall in battle than live on defeated.
At the end, Mara gives up. His lute slips from under his arm, and he disappears. So Rohatsu isn't only endurance.
It's the same scene played again, in a cold hall, by ordinary people, the troops arriving on schedule and named as they come.

how: In Japanese Zen, monasteries and practice groups keep Rohatsu as a week of intensive sitting that ends on the day observed as the Buddha's awakening.

a Zen week of sitting that ends on awakening day

games.q: the week of sitting: tap the pairs.
p: says kindly: why wear yourself out?

s: in the poem, Mara's army is a host of monsters with weapons
the seeker names it: desires, discontent, hunger and thirst, craving, sleepiness, fear, doubt.
in the Padhana Sutta, Mara begins kindly
he tells the seeker to live and do good deeds instead of striving.
the poem tells the seeker to drive the army off by force
he meets it with wisdom, like a stone breaking an unbaked pot: he sees each troop, names it, and stays.

games.q: you're the seeker, thin from striving, and a kind voice says: live, do good deeds, why wear yourself out? what do you do?
o: agree, and go do good deeds instead
name what's speaking, and keep going
argue that you aren't tired at all
games.why: the seeker names Mara's army troop by troop and stays. in the end Mara's lute slips from his arm and he disappears.

practice: As each thing turns up, name it quietly with the poem's words: desire, discontent, hunger, sleepiness, fear, doubt. Name it, and stay where you are. You don't have to win; you only have to notice and not get up.

wordCard.voice: Rohatsu. The Zen week of sitting that ends on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening, when the old army comes and gets named. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit Māra: the tempter who, in the poem, leads the army of desire and doubt.

carryVoice: Your line: the week of sitting. The army comes, and the seeker stays. Back tomorrow, same hill.
